utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would His Honour turn the microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Let me just introduce myself as a new face to this Tribunal and as a new face to all of you. I am Judge Agius, as you probably already know, I come from Malta, and I look forward to working with the team of the Prosecution, the team of the Defence, two teams of the Defence, in this quite difficult case, I must say. I haven't been extremely lucky in the allotment of -- allocation of the case compared to my other colleagues, but this is something that I am used to. In my career of 25 years as a judge in my country, the last 15 of which at the highest level, as a court of last instance, I have been dealing with practically the worst cases that have come up before the courts in Malta. Before I proceed with the few things that I would like to tell you today, I want to make sure that the accused are hearing me and that they can understand what I am saying in a language -- in their own language or in a language that they can understand. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me, and can you understand me in your own language? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, can you hear and understand me in your own language. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I can understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed, I would also like to confirm the appearances as they have been indicated to me, and I would start first with appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, together with Anna Richterova, who sits to my right, also assisted by the case manager, Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And appearances for accused Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, welcome to the Tribunal, and we're delighted to have you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you are not unlucky. You have drawn a very good case and you will find that it's a pleasure to deal with those of us who are representing the accused, at least, and perhaps even Ms. Korner. I am John Ackerman. I represent Mr. Brdjanin. And with me today is translator Ava Mirkovic and my legal assistant, Mr. Milos Peric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Welcome to this case. I represent General Talic. My name is Michel Pitron. I'm being assisted by Ms. Natasha Fauveau. I have another colleague who sometimes comes to the hearings, that is Mr. Xavier de Roux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Let me start from here, and I will try to be short. I am quite familiar with your faces, because as soon as I was assigned the case, having had some experience back home with inheriting cases, the first thing I did, I asked for a video recording of the previous sittings so that I could take stock of what exactly happened, also because of the various pieces and bits and pieces of information that was being fed to me by my legal assistants and by others in this Tribunal. But the most important reason for doing so was precisely because rather than following the previous proceedings by going through piles and piles and papers, it was easier, and I have always found it easier to follow it on the screen. So I am -- let me assure you not with just your faces but also with all that has gone under the bridges in these last months including, in particular, the last Status Conference which I had the pleasure of watching again this morning in my apartment for the third time. Let me make things clear. I am in the habit of putting first things first, and according to me, the most important thing in this trial before we even start it and later on when we start it to ensure that the two accused will have a fair trial, will not only have a fair trial but will also have a fair trial in the shortest time possible. That is priority number one on my agenda. Number two is that I realise that during the past sessions, hearings, sittings, there may have been some friction, some misunderstanding sometimes between the Prosecution team and the two teams for the Defence, sometimes between either or both of you and the Presiding Judge. I have gone carefully through all that has happened, and it is my idea today to suggest to you to leave what has happened in the past, not exactly forget all about it, but try to look forward once the journey lies ahead rather than look backwards and try to repeat or start all over again things that have actually contributed to this pre-trial stage into becoming sometimes an arena for misunderstanding and for -- let's leave it at misunderstanding and not choose any further words. I am starting more or less with a clean slate, and my offer to you is one of full cooperation to bring to an end this pre-trial stage within the shortest possible time and proceed again within the shortest possible time to the commencement of the trial. As you know, a trial date has been set for January 21st and I think it is my duty to echo and repeat what Judge Hunt, my predecessor, has made clear in the last hearing that unless there are very, very serious considerations, the Chamber will be very reluctant to entertain any suggestions or proposals or motions for a delay in the beginning of the trial. So this is something which I am keen on and something which will be at the back of my mind as we go along. I am, of course, prepared to listen to everything that you have to say, and it is my proposal to you today to go step by step and review the situation in this Pre-Trial Conference on each and every aspect that I think ought to be discussed and cleared during this sitting, and following this Pre-Trial Conference, then we will have, I hope, a short final Status Conference before we can then start with the trial as such. I conclude by saying that I think and I feel sure, at least I am assured but my legal and clerical staff that I have in my possession all the documentation as of today including the revised fourth amendment and including the translation of the various motions that the Defence of General Talic have presented. I had read them in French which I understand but I don't speak very well. I will try to follow what you have to say in French sometimes and by the end of the trial, I'll probably be as fluent as you are, but I will try and cover as much territory as we can today. Please bear with me if this hearing will be a long one, but I think it ought to be as long as necessary so that we try and cover all the terrain that we need to before we proceed for the trial. I would like the Defence, the two Defence teams to confirm to me whether they have received this morning the copy of the amended text of the fourth amended indictment. The fourth amended indictment was corrected or updated in terms or in accordance with Judge Hunt's decision of the 23rd of November. The copy was delivered to me this morning and I would like to know whether the Defence is in possession. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received it as I arrived at the court. I haven't had a chance to look at it and of course my client, Mr. Brdjanin, has not seen it and can't until it's been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We find ourselves in that same situation, Your Honour. I received in the documents when I came into the courtroom so I was not able to read it nor was my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was expecting to hear because I would have probably complimented you had you told me that you had gone through it and confirmed that the changes to it were in accordance with Judge Hunt's decision. However, my legal staff has gone through it in the course of the morning and they assure me, although I don't want to feel bound by what I am saying, they assure me that it is in conformity, it has been changed, the amendments to it are in accordance with Judge Hunt's decision of November 23. Before I move to the matter of disclosures, is there anything that either the team for the Prosecution or teams for the Defence would like to add with regard to the indictment? I know, Mr. Pitron, that you have filed an appeal against the decision of the 23rd of November regarding the amendments to -- and I have also seen your pre-trial brief as it relates, in part, to the same merit that forms part of your appeal application or appeal motion. Would you like to add anything in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I think things are clear as they are. That's as you said. We appealed the decision rendered by Judge Hunt in respect of the last indictment. We also filed an application for dismissal of charges and an application for setting aside of various stages of the procedures. I believe that you have all those documents and therefore you're in a position to be familiar with the very fully explained position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing: I'm very pleased with the way you have responded to my question. My style of conducting proceedings - I think it's only fair to advise you about it - is that I can assure you that each and every document that is presented, I go through several times, from the first word to the last, so you can expect me to come here in the courtroom fully familiar with the contents of each and every document. When the document consists in submissions, one thing that more or less sometimes irritates me is that it is then followed by oral submissions which essentially repeat almost verbatim the contents of the written submission. I have been taught as a young judge many years ago that I ought to make allowances because I have to concede, and as an ex-defence lawyer, I know exactly what it means, that my client used to expect me -- expect to hear me say something, and something really worth hearing, in open court. So that you can rest assured that I understand, and you will find me very cooperative. However, I appeal to your sense of cooperation, of which I am a hundred per cent sure, from what I have seen and from what I am seeing now, that there may be times when I will call upon you to cut short and not repeat unduly what is already contained in a written document. I will do that only when I feel that you are overstepping what I would expect to be reasonable. Of course, I will leave you all doors open for airing anything new that is not contained, in other words, in the written documents, or anything that you may have thought -- you may think ought to be stated by way of clarification or better explanation of what is contained in the written statements or written memoranda. I think we will get used to each other. I'm telling you this because this is a trial, like many other trials, where a lot of cooperation is necessary and where we have necessarily to be patient with one another, and therefore I'm telling you this beforehand so that you will know more or less where you stand with me. Disclosure. I know that this was a hotly debated issue during the last Status Conference, and I want to make sure that all outstanding matters related to disclosure will be concluded today. Let me first put a question to Ms. Korner with regard to Rule 66(A). Is it the intention or is the Prosecution planning to call any additional witnesses apart from those which have already been declared?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I answer Your Honour's question, could I just ask Your Honour for clarification on one matter that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you had received translations of all of the motions made by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We haven't. We've had a translation only of the appeal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I have -- mind you, I received these roughly about two hours ago, and I have the application for leave to appeal --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which I suppose you have. Then I have the translation of the request to dismiss charges, which was filed on the 7th of December, and also the -- the dismiss charges I do not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's two -- like Your Honour, I read French, although my spoken French, regrettably, has disintegrated. The second motion is to dismiss anything to do with Talic and the ARK Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to give you a brief summary of the documents we're speaking about in order to expedite matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Pitron, I have your document in French. I simply don't have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They were made available this morning. It could well be that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't want to waste Your Honour's time on this matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, but it is important, because although these will -- the motions themselves can still be dealt with in the original language. On the other hand, I fully endorse much of the complaints that have been forthcoming from both sides in the course of the former proceedings, that each one of you should be put in a position where they can feel that they are -- they have come here prepared to deal with whatever needs to be dealt with. And I realise that in many instances, if there is a document which has not yet been translated and which is on the day's or on the sitting's agenda, that could create problems. I mean, I understand, for example, had, on your part, you come up with problems with regard to the changes to the fourth amended indictment, I would have probably had an answer ready for you. But with regard to translations and all that, of some very important documents, I quite agree they should be made available. I have told you that I have had mine barely two hours ago. I asked for them last week, before I embarked on my weekend enjoyment, and all I know is that I was informed that they were translated today and they were ready. But I'm sure that the registrar will see to it that they are handed to Ms. Korner as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure, if they were only translated this morning, there's a system by way that they're given to the various people involved, and it obviously hasn't gone through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have. I can lend you mine if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would simply say although I was going to make a suggestion to Your Honour about motions once the trial had started, that I hoped that Your Honour wasn't going to ask me to deal with them orally today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, of course not. Of course not. I do realise that. But my idea was to have those motions that could be disposed of prior to the commencement of the trial itself, I will dispose of. That very much depends on the exchange of written submissions or replies or whatever and whether there will be any further hearings required which, frankly, I don't think of. I mean the -- Mr. Pitron's motions are quite detailed. They are in a way reflected also sometimes word for word also in his pre-trial brief. In other words, I mean there is a lot of common ground. My intention is to have everything ready before the trial starts. So the -- you will find me cooperative obviously, and I would appeal to cooperation from your side as well so that you will put me in a position where I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly. I mean the reason that we don't answer them when they're lengthy like that until we get a translation is although we can read French we're not altogether sure we've got the right nuances. May I just mention at this stage I know Your Honour's asked a question which I'm going to answer. It would be my suggestion because of this difficulty of translations that once the trial starts, so that all counsel are here, of course when counsel are in the United States and France and here it's difficult, that the application should be made orally with a skeleton argument in advance because otherwise, if they are in writing, we go through this -- the same problem each time that each side waits for a translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- whereas in open court we have the translators available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is very true and that's a very practical approach, I must say, Ms. Korner, and I hope the message is taken. Of course I am in not in a position to control the presence of each and every, I mean I'm pretty sure that Mr. de Roux, if he's not here today, he has got his good reasons and I wouldn't even ask what these good reasons are. I've worked with lawyers all my life and as an ex-lawyer myself, I know that more or less if there is the -- an entente cordial between the Defence, Prosecution, and the Judge and there is always the assumption that everyone operates in good faith and to the best of his or her ability, then most of the time there is no need for questions asked for questions answered. Still, I realise the importance of the presence of each and every person. I also notice that there is a change in face during the last Status Conference. You were flanked on your right by a gentleman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who is not here today. Is Mr. Cayley still a member of the team?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. As Mr. Ackerman never fails to point out, the Prosecution team has a number of lawyers attached to it all doing different things at various different times. Mr. Cayley is a senior trial attorney like myself, but at present is not here. I mean he's not in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My first question was whether you have any additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and I was about to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As we notified the Defence and as Your Honour knows, because there's a motion for protective measures in respect of witnesses 4. for whom the Prosecution’s latest motion for protective measures refers I don't 5 know how familiar Your Honour is from Your Honour's researches with the problems of calling such witnesses. The only reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know we dealt with the problem in the preparatory commission works for the International Criminal Court and having heard Amnesty International, for example, or Red Cross, I know exactly what the problems are. I have also read your motion for protective measures with regard to the witnesses that are referred to there. It was my intention to come to that at a later stage, but because I take it -- when I'm asking you whether you have any additional witnesses, I am not referring to those. I am asking you to take that for granted that those will be additional witnesses, the only question remaining being whether and to what extent they should be protected and what kind of protective measures. So additional witnesses means other additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honour, there are statements or the other witnesses are experts who are referred to in the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I am coming to experts later on. Expert witnesses and forensic witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I'm coming to that later on. Apart from those, any additional?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be a statement from the lead investigator in this case who will deal with where the documents, each of the documents in the exhibit list comes from plus a general overview of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a person whose name --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is mentioned on the -- I'm not sure he's mentioned but he's the lead investigator. I'm not sure his name is mentioned in the pre-trial brief. It's more certainly to allow the Defence to know where each document that we are using emanates from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is a pleasure yet to come for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. We've had the investigator going through the list but in fact, they know -- they should know already because as they've been disclosed. They've been told what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I have a commitment on your part that this will be something that will be concluded before the trial starts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, certainly. I -- Your Honour, every time I've said by a certain date, for one reason or another something's gone wrong but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not querying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- it will be disclosed before, I hope, the Christmas adjournment. In addition to that, Your Honour, there is one statement that relates purely, if I use the expression "crime-base evidence," which we hope would be disclosed by Friday of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is this to be covered by some protective, demand for protective measure or not or is it just a clear-cut ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say this? I can't say that at the moment because the statement is, at the moment, being taken in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's to deal with one matter that we've been unable to cover so far by direct evidence although it's been covered by indirect evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition, does Your Honour wish me to move on or to raise topics yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I would rather prefer to raise topics myself and then obviously whatever I miss which I -- which you point out to me and I will come back to it. But I do have what my intention is to take topic by topic. At the moment, we are talking of discussing disclosure and before concluding on that, well obviously I will ask you whether you have anything else to add or to comment on to say. Okay? During the last Status Conference, Ms. Korner, the conclusion was that not all witness statements had been disclosed to the Defence, and it was very clear that the reason for that was not a shortcoming on the part of the Defence but a problem of translation. Has that problem been solved or is there reason to believe that the Defence have not yet received the totality of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me one moment while I just find out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, if Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Pitron, if you can remember or you can think of any witness statement that you expected to be handed to you by today and hasn't been handed over or you are expecting it, please let me know. It will help put the Prosecution in a better picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, as I understand it of the translations of the disclosed witness statements from English into the Bosnian language, there's only one, possibly two still not received back from the translation unit. Your Honour, there are all sorts of problems associated with translation, one of which is particular, and perhaps I ought to raise it straight away. Your Honour, in relation to a witness who produced a lengthy diary about -- both Defence applied to have Your Honour exclude it because it wasn't translated, I'm sorry, not Your Honour, the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a moment I was going to feel happy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We told the Trial Chamber and those defending that 600 pages of that diary would be translated by the 21st of January when the trial started. We did so because that is what we were told and we had it in writing from the translation unit. What was not appreciated by the translation unit was that these pages were typed, and we've received a second memo which I have somewhere, Your Honour, dated the 7th of December which state that, "One page of the original document which is single spaced with no margins works out to almost two standard pages in translation. The total figure of 1.800 original pages therefore is closer to 3.500 standard pages in translation." They say that they can produce 600 standard pages by the 21st. They were talking about translation unit standard pages, but that, as I understand it, means for the actual reality only 300 pages. There's then, I don't think I need to trouble Your Honour with what's the discussion at how further translation is to be achieved at this stage, but I wish to correct straight away that we said 600 pages. I hope it is accepted that we said so in all innocence judging by what the translation unit said. So ready by the 21st of January only 300 pages. Your Honour, I do however reiterate that because of this, although the evidence will be taken out of context, as it were, because we intend to start with the Banja Luka municipality, nonetheless the witness will not give evidence until such time as we have achieved translation of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, I quite appreciate that. I also appreciate the difficulties that this Tribunal encounters generally with translation problems and how that affects the important task that you have to carry. Still, I'm sure that you also appreciate, and you will cooperate with me and the other two Judges who will be joining me in this trial later on, in trying to have all the relevant, necessary documentation readily available the day the trial commences. I will be later on appealing to you to organise the trial from the Prosecution point of view. You will be conducting your own case to start with, and therefore you necessarily have to make out a plan, and what I have just said enters within that plan. In other words, if the diary and the contents of the diary become important not in the first stage of the trial but in a subsequent, later stage of the trial, then you are going to find me very cooperative in that. If, instead, there is reason to believe that the contents -- or knowledge of the contents of that diary may be important for the Defence in following and contesting what is done, what happens in the first stage of the trial, then I want to make sure that that diary is available before or immediately the trial starts, because that is very important. I mean, I repeat: I come from the defence, and I have spent the last 15, 18 years of my career deciding criminal cases in the criminal jurisdiction but also in the constitutional human rights due process context, and I attach a lot of importance to what I consider to be correct by way of due process and a fair trial. And I know you will not be impressed, because now it's catching up also in the United Kingdom, the French are more familiar with it, the Americans, of course, have got the experience of the Supreme Court. But I feel inspired all along by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights, and in my work, I try to follow the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights, not because they are binding on this Tribunal but because I consider them to contain the principles which a good judge feels he or she ought to follow. This is basically it. So I think I'm making myself understood. Anything -- I appreciate that you are going to have your first phase of the trial, your second, your third, fourth, or whatever. I am going to put my trust completely in your hands that you will make sure that the Defence will have all the documentation necessary to be able to start and follow the trial in its first stage, from very day one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet, but can I just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mention something before he does say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does she have your permission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The situation with the diary is that we are attempting -- we are going to make all attempts to get this translated somehow or other. If necessary, we will alter the plan of the trial, although it does make more sense, because Banja Luka is the major, as it were, the hub of what happens, to start that. I should add: We can at least get summaries of the contents, and at least the accused know what's in it because they can read the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I think this matter came up before. Already it was mentioned, and I understand there was an objection on the part of the Defence for General Talic. So unless the position of counsel for General Talic has changed, I would suggest you do not go into it. What I was going to suggest is that I'm sure that in your team you have several who are conversant with the B/C/S and who can assume the responsibility of identifying from that diary the various parts that require to be translated, not just from your point of view but also from the Defence point of view, before anything else, because I'm sure that -- when I was very young, I used to keep a diary myself, but there were important entries and less important entries. I mean, I remember when I used to play football, and I used to put every Saturday and every Sunday how many scores, how many goals I would have scored that weekend. Looking back today, that's not important, but there are other things that are important. They were important then and they are still important now. And I would suppose that that way, if you think you can rely entirely on your B/C/S-speaking members of your team and assume the responsibility of having translated all that you think is important, then you will be putting yourself in a situation where the Defence would definitely find it difficult to argue that they were not given the totality, et cetera. Because if the rest is not important, it's not important in the beginning and it will remain not important until the very end. I mean, if it's not important. But it's a responsibility that you must be prepared to carry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tell Your Honour, I didn't want to interrupt, but that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The pages that have gone in for translation are not simply that we've started with page 1. We have selected from having had members of the team read through those pages which appear to be relevant to the case. The 600 that we had selected covered the period between April 1992 and I think it was September, which are the major events. So we've done that. But the Defence rightly say they want translation of the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have a right. They definitely have a right. But then obviously every right is relative. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. Sorry for having kept you waiting for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem at all. I think it might be helpful for you to have some context with regard to this whole problem of documents. The Prosecution, when they provide us with documents, generally have a chart which lists all the documents that have been provided, and that chart will say, for instance, that documents were disclosed on 7 December 2001. That's the date that the Prosecutor puts them in a package and sends them toward me. Now, I may not get them for several days after that. I won't get these 7th of December documents actually in my hands until next week sometime. Some of them will be in English and some of them will be B/C/S. I can't read the B/C/S, of course. What happens once they arrive at my office is they go through a process that involves putting them through a scanner, getting them computerised, things like that. They are then organised and sent to Banja Luka, where the people whose job it is to investigate what's contained in those documents and to read them, if they can, if they're in B/C/S, it's their job then to start that process. So from the time the Prosecutor sends me a document on December 7th until my people in Banja Luka can even begin the process of dealing with it can be as long as 30 or 40 days, depending on the number of documents. For instance, within the last 30 or 40 days, I've been served with about 6.300 papers of purely witness material. That doesn't include exhibits and things like that. It takes an enormous amount of time just to process those 6.300 pages and then to get them to Banja Luka, and then they have to go through them all. And just sitting down and reading 6.300 pages of material takes days and days, and so we're dealing with that kind of a problem. Now, the Prosecutor tells you that it is their intention to begin this trial with the Banja Luka municipality. I spent the entire day yesterday working on that very issue, on those very witnesses. I can tell you there are a number of documents that are either English only or B/C/S only that are contained within those materials dealing with the Banja Luka municipality. So there are some documents in the Prosecution materials that I can't read, and there are some documents that my people in Banja Luka can't read, and if that's the case when this trial starts in a few days, we will be terribly handicapped. Because when the Prosecution calls a witness, we should at least have had the opportunity to read the material supplied with regard to that witness and conduct whatever investigation might be necessary to prepare for cross-examination of that witness. So what I foresee, for instance, with Banja Luka municipality, this 2.000-page diary that we've been talking about that I can't read deals with the Banja Luka municipality for a two-year period, a period that's crucial to this indictment. Judge Hunt said in his order - he was very prescient about that - that once I have an opportunity to read that, it may be necessary that a number of witnesses be recalled for further cross-examination because there were things in that diary that I would have asked those witnesses had I known about it. So what I foresee is that we're going to have -- we're going to first of all start with the worst possible municipality for trying to deal with that 2.000-page document, if we started with Banja Luka, but I also recognise it's the logical place for the Prosecutor to start this case. The translation problems are enormous. I have -- I will turn over within the next day or two a large number of documents to the Tribunal's translation department, and who knows when those might be done. But I can't even think of providing them to the Prosecution until I know what they say, and I won't know what they say until they've been translated, because I might not want to use them as evidence. So the translation problems are enormous, Judge, and I don't want them to be minimised, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not minimising them in the least. I am fully aware of them, and that's why I started off telling you earlier on today, in the beginning of this hearing, that I have gone through the video recordings of the previous sittings, because this problem seems to be endemic, and it's a big problem. Mr. Pitron, I expect you fully endorse what Mr. Ackerman has said. I'm just calling upon you to see whether you would like to add anything to what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I share fully what Mr. Ackerman said. I would like to emphasise one point, however, which I believe is very important. We began by saying that you would emphasise the absolute necessary, you say the absolute priority was to have respect for the rights of the accused and I'm very pleased by what you said because I am of those who believe that the necessary respect for the rights of the accused is one which allows for excellent justice to be rendered. There is a fundamental point and all of us know that, that is Defence cannot be understood, appreciated, except in overall terms. We can understand what direction to give the -- to the strategy that we are going to have, how we are going to cross-examine the witnesses only if we know all of what the Prosecutor is going to bring forward, that is to have translations, full translations of what we are -- we are now encountering a very serious problem, that is the most of the Prosecutors exhibits were disclosed recently to us. I'm not saying that they were late because you asked us not to enter into polemics. This morning, I received a list that is -- that is the start of the afternoon a list of new statements and to hear the Prosecutor telling me now that I will receive a list saying that it has new statements of former witnesses and I hear the witness -- Prosecutor saying that there was to be a few more that were going to come. I am in a very difficult position now to put up a consistent defence all the more so because all of these documents that I received from the Prosecution to date are documents which they have had a long time, at least most of them. Sometimes I am disturbed, I'm bothered because I wonder whether the Prosecutor didn't have the time to study the documents, was the Prosecutor in a hurry and that's -- maybe that's the reason I received them late or has he -- has she been keeping them for a reason, I don't know why, and giving them to me late. So that puts me in a difficult position and makes it difficult for me to understand them and to respond, and that's what I wanted to emphasise. I need to see all of the Prosecutor's documents and I very officially am requesting once again, I'm asking the Prosecutor to tell us definitively when disclosure will be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are basically turning back to you, Ms. Korner. From what I gather, the outstanding disclosure matters relate to a statement from the lead investigator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is -- should be forthcoming soon, another statement which is crime-based evidence which should materialise this week, then there are one or two statements that still require to be translated and then forwarded to the Defence, and this humungous diary translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are still some outstanding translations that have been outstanding for some time relating to documents but, Your Honour, one of the difficulties has been, and it's perhaps a difference of expression between the parties, is that these statements are made by the Defence about new statements being served this morning, and in their response to the pre-trial brief there were various allegations about lateness. It may well be that the two offices are counting in different ways, but let's put it at that. Your Honour, what has to be done under the Rules is that where we call a witness, we have to search through the material held in this Tribunal which, as Your Honour can appreciate, is massive over the last eight years or so to see whether that witness is mentioned in other statements or has made statements to other authorities which, without making the search, we're not aware of when we had to do a number of searches. What was disclosed this morning were the searches, the material that relates to witnesses that the Defence already have the statements of who we have said that we intend to call, and this is the material that has been produced. Those searches, Your Honour, are -- we have completed searches in respect of 109 of the witnesses we intend to call. 32 searches have been completed but have not been reviewed because obviously a lot of material that is thrown up is wholly irrelevant and one of the complaints from the Defence has been that we are giving them irrelevant material. There are 42 searches still to be completed. That material will all be disclosed before the trial starts but we have not disclosed any new witness statements this morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm referring to Rule 68, disclosures, exculpatory, is there any?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the outstanding matters are that, again, there are searches being conducted not of statements but of what can be described as.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is in addition to what you have just stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are now talking Rule 68 entirely. We have completed the Rule 68 disclosure of all documentary material and the like that we know about. Your Honour, may I say, you can never say we've disclosed every single exculpatory document we've had because there's just too much of it, but we never stop making sure that we've done it. But as a final, as it were, search, we are looking at notes kept by investigators of conversations with people, not signed statements which may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Banja Luka interviews that were mentioned during the previous --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, we've dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can I very briefly explain? Your Honour, obviously the investigations particularly into this part of Bosnia have been going on since 1994. During the course of those investigations, clearly hundreds of people have been spoken to by investigators and notes made of what they say, but for one reason or another, statements were never taken or signed statements were never taken. We are now attempting, and I use the word because there's a mass of stuff to go through, all that material to see if there are, contained in those notes, material which could be potentially exculpatory of these two accused. Your Honour, as I say, we could never really say we ever finally put a stop to Rule 68 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I realise that. I realise also that knowing that there is a responsibility on your part. You do exactly what other prosecutors in other countries with the same system do. Just make sure that you have as much in your hands which necessarily means that you will be passing on the baby to the other side sometimes that have to decide what is exculpatory and what is not. And I understand also that although the Defence may have its -- their complaints on this, in reality, I am sure they also understand that this is something that more or less is almost unavoidable. But anyway, I will come to that at a later stage. So more or less what you're telling the Tribunal is that the discovery stage with regard to Rule 68 matters, material is still underway, it's nearly completion, and that it's not completed because you are trying to reduce as -- minimise the exercise or reduce the number of materials that make --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- Your Honour may be slightly -- I won't say confusing two matters. The witnesses that we've served, we're giving all the material whether it's Rule 68 or whatever if it's relevant. In other words, if the witness made a statement to the -- to another country's authorities, that they get that even if it says more or less the same thing. If a witness has testified before, which, in this court, a number of them have, then they get all of that material as well. So that's what the searches involve. The Rule 68 material, we have searched through all the document collections that appear to be relevant to this case and completed Rule 68 on that. As we understand the Defence, as Your Honour will have seen, it's not very clear from either of the pre-trial briefs that the Defence have served exactly what the Defence is other than a complete denial, and that doesn't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this: There are two pre-trial briefs from the Defence, one from Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin which is a mere three pages and more or less it outlines, in a very concise way, the main arguments or the various types of denial. On the part of General Talic, it's a much more detailed pre-trial brief which also enters into the legal aspects which Mr. Ackerman reserved for later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to raise those pre-trial briefs at some stage. If Your Honour wants me to deal with them now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By way of reciprocal disclosure or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's another topic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Okay. Let's jump and you can raise it now and perhaps we can deal -- but leave out the reciprocal disclosure matter because I think you can reach a compromise between the two of you on that if you reduce it to the basics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I leave that topic for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will have seen that we've put in a response to the pre-trial brief that was supplied by Mr. Ackerman. Your Honour, on the basis that we -- it is our view, particularly given the detail that we went into in our pre-trial brief, that it is an inadequate response and does not comply with the rule. Now, Your Honour, I'm not asking Your Honour to make a ruling on that at the moment. Your Honour's seen what we have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I will definitely not make a ruling on it mostly because I will tell you in very plain language that had I been Mr. Brdjanin's Defence counsel, I would have probably done exactly the same. I prefer not to go into greater detail at this stage, but Mr. Ackerman's pre-trial brief more or less corresponds with what I think ought to be a pre-trial brief on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the difficulty is that both Your Honour and I come from jurisdictions where it was not incumbent upon the Defence to give the Prosecution any indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not exactly but you can't extract from the Defence beforehand the -- specifically the line, because you know, we have all lived trials and sometimes -- I am sure that you come from the Defence as well, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I am not going to teach any one of you but you know how things change in a trial and all of a sudden, a trial will take a twist and a turning that was completely unexpected, and you have to have all the presence of mind and legal knowledge and sense of pragmatism and practice to adapt yourself to the circumstance and the situation as it arises be it the Prosecution who has to suffer this or be it the Defence. And this is why I believe that the less one ties himself or herself to very, very specific parameters by way of line of Defence or whatever, the better it is. I mean I would have done -- I mean I do not intend to praise Mr. Ackerman's pre-trial brief, but I mean it's not far from what I would have expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course although our rules in the United Kingdom have changed slightly, and one of the reasons they have changed is because it's thought right that the fairness of a trial is fairness for all sides, that is, the State who bring the Prosecution who act on behalf of the people, and in International Tribunals for, as it were, all States, and the Defence. And it is no longer thought right and clearly that is why this rule was promulgated that the Defence should be able to take the Prosecution by surprise, by surprising not revealing what its Defence was. And if Your Honour looks at the Rule, which is Rule 65 ter (F), Your Honour will see that in general terms -- what must be set out is in general terms the nature of the accused's defence, the matter which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief and in the case of such matter, the reason. Now, Your Honour, I don't want to go through our -- Your Honour said earlier we needn't go through our written submissions, but that has not happened. Your Honour, in respect of -- can I leave Mr. Brdjanin's pre-trial brief or Mr. Ackerman's because I think, as I say we've set out clearly what we say has not happened. We haven't responded in writing. We have not responded in writing to the pre-trial brief on behalf of Momir Talic as yet, and indeed perhaps I can deal with the points now that we submit have not been covered, rather than yet again in writing, and therefore causing translation problems. Your Honour, one of the major aspects of the Prosecution case against General Talic - or not one, but certainly a significant one - is the running of a camp called Manjaca. No response is given in the pre-trial brief which even mentions Manjaca. There is nothing about whether or not, although we've had this discussion before, international armed conflict is going to be an issue in this case, equally not in Mr. Ackerman's brief, exhumations, and nothing really about the law at all. Your Honour, if the answer is that General Talic accepts the allegations that we make about Manjaca, that is well and good, but I would consider that it's most unlikely that he does. Your Honour wishes to leave reciprocal disclosure for later, but Your Honour, in our submission, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I would prefer you to go straight into -- if you have concluded on the part regarding your response or your reaction to General Talic pre-trial brief, then you can move to the reciprocal disclosure matter and deal with it, so that then I can ask Mr. Pitron to reply to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honours, of course the sanction is that they would not be allowed to call evidence if it's not shown that it's disputed. Your Honour, reciprocal disclosure, both accused invoked the provisions of Rule 66(B) and it's been discussed on a number of occasions in the Status Conferences. We wrote to both accused on the 1st of November, asking them to provide us with any material they intended to use as evidence. We've had no response from either accused, or the Defence for either accused, and I think that for what Mr. Ackerman says, the response is going to be "I don't know what documents I'm going to be using because they have not been translated yet." Well, it may well be that they have not been translated, but I assume that, like us, Mr. Ackerman - and I know he has co-counsel who come from the Republika Srpska - must be able to tell Mr. Ackerman what is in those documents and whether or not they are likely to be used in trial. Your Honour, the rules are here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's with regard to Mr. Brdjanin's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to General Talic's pre-trial brief, do you have any reciprocal disclosure issue raised or not? COUNSEL: Yes, Your Honour. We've written to both men, saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but with regard to Mr. Ackerman, you've more or less -- had stated that already formally in your reply to his --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to General Talic, since there is no written replies yet, I haven't understood so far that you are claiming that there is a reciprocal disclosure issue as well. Are you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm sorry. I hoped I was dealing with it in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've had no response from counsel for General Talic in respect to our request, and we would be - can I put it this way - slightly surprised if there was no documentation that the Defence for General Talic intended to produce during the course of the trial. Again, Your Honour, the same principle applies: Although Mr. Pitron and Mr. de Roux may not speak the language, Madam Fauveau does, and therefore, again, they must know what is in the documents and whether they're likely to use them or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me suggest to take these issues one by one, and I call on Mr. Ackerman first to address the reciprocal disclosure issue first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very simply, the Rule requires me to disclose to the Prosecution any document that I intend to use as evidence. I have not yet identified any document that I intend to use as evidence. I have some documents that I can read, and I know what they say, and there's at least the possibility that some of them are evidentiary material. I have, as I mentioned earlier, a very large number of documents that I just received that will be sent off to translation, so I can determine exactly what the contents of those are. I have no idea whether I'll use even one of them as an exhibit or not. If Judge Hunt's estimate of how far away we are from starting the Defence case is anywhere near correct, it's a long time before the Prosecutor's case ends. A lot of what we might decide to use as Defence evidence will depend on what happens in the Prosecution's case. It may be that it's not necessary to provide certain exhibits because cross-examination may be successful to a point where providing exhibits would be a waste of the Court's time. I will assure the Court of this: At the exact moment that I make a determination to use a document in evidence, I will get copies of it, both in B/C/S and English, to the Prosecutor in as timely a manner as I possibly can, which will probably be very quick, but I can't at this point give them documents that I think there is the remote possibility that I might use as evidence if I don't even know what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that satisfactory to you, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that means that before a witness is about to be - for the Prosecution - is about to be cross-examined on a document, the day before or an hour before we're given a copy of that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is what Mr. Ackerman means, then I will be very cross with him, and I am sure from reading not just between the lines, but if -- I am pretty sure that that's not what he meant. You said that you were going to do your absolute best to be able to identify these items of evidence, whatever they may be, and as they may prove to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I had a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- do your duty in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I had a document that I knew I was going to use in the cross-examination of one of the Banja Luka witnesses, I'd give it to them today. I don't have such a document, I just don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron, are you more or less in the same waters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't speak at length. I cannot allow the Prosecution to say that General Talic is the reason for the delay as regards disclosure. I simply recall that when I submitted our pre-trial brief, I still did not have the Tribunal's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Tribunal is definitely not seeing where it could put any blame on your client for any delay that there has been or there might be. Your client is certainly not to blame, so you don't need to convince me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about myself, not my client, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... even more than that, because I have had the opportunity to follow what you are been doing so far, you and Mr. de Roux, and I have no reason to complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]: Very briefly, then. Until very recently, I did not have a final or definitive indictment. That was a very important point, that is, the charges against General Talic as to whether or not he was a member of the ARK, of the Crisis Staff. The issue has still not been resolved, because it has been sent to the Appeals Chamber, and therefore, under such circumstances it is difficult for me to take a position, as I've already said, in respect of a Defence strategy. In the same way, until very recently, and I still don't have all of the documents which I can understand myself and which my client can understand in order to set out a Defence strategy. That's the only reason why, despite myself, I have been unable to disclose to the Prosecution all the documents that it's asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine that there must be some documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you are in a position to disclose in any case, I mean irrespective of the problems that have arisen and that you have very rightly referred to. Because I realise that there is an appeal pending. I realise that there has been and there continues to be the question relating to the ARK crisis group. I do understand -- I was complaining myself, until last Friday, that I did not have an updated copy of the latest version of the indictment, so I fully sympathise with -- I also understand that there are problems which are endemic to -- and not just relating to this case, but which permiate the whole operation in this Tribunal, all the work in this Tribunal. The Tribunal is plagued with certain problems on which neither you, nor Ms. Korner, nor Mr. Ackerman, nor anyone else has got control, unfortunately, and we have to live with those. So there are times when one has to close a blind eye and move ahead. The most important thing for me is, and let me make myself clear, and this is not -- I am not suggesting anything to you or to Mr. Ackerman or to Ms. Korner, et cetera. What I don't want is anyone to take advantage of the unfortunate situation that we find ourselves in and play a game. This is what I want to avoid. I am not saying -- and for the moment, I definitely do not suspect that Ms. Korner or Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Pitron, any one of you three are playing this game or that you intend to play this game. But it is also important that whatever is at the moment within your possession and which you could let the other side have by way of discovery, please do it, because then if you don't, there will be problems later on, and this is what I want to avoid. What I am all the way appealing to you to do with me is to forget about things that have happened in the past in this case, and let's start fresh. I said I'm starting with a clean slate, and so are you. Let's forget the past and concentrate on the future. I know that there have been instances where there were complaints coming from the Prosecution that they had written to you and you had not replied, or that you had refused to do what, in the opinion of the Prosecution, they would have expected you to accept. I know that this has happened. They happen everywhere. They happen all the time. I'm used to this. But there comes a time when you realise, or everyone should realise, that the case is going to start. It's going to start on the 21st of January, and it may well be important at this stage, and before the 21st of January, to have a more practical approach. I understand and I fully agree with you that you may not be in a position to disclose all the material that the Prosecution in one way or another expects. That I fully understand. But I also -- I am also fully confident that you must have in your possession material which you can disclose at this point in time, pending further disclosures later on as the material becomes known to you and as it becomes available. And this is my appeal to you. If between now and the trial you think that you will have or you would have identified material which ought to be disclosed, then I appeal to you to make an open commitment or make a commitment in open Court today with the Tribunal to do that so that we try to lessen the divergences that there may be between the two parties. Then I can assure you will have every opportunity to fight it out between you during the trial and that I will enjoy every single minute of it while you are at it. In the meantime, please don't take a rigid position. If there is material that you can, in all honestly, disclose, please do it, because you will make the life of each and every one of you, and including my own, less difficult. I wouldn't say easier, but certainly less difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour wouldn't care to make an order to that effect, that before the 21st --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I mean my problem is this: that I very much sympathise with the Defence at this point in time that they may well truly be in a position which they would be taking great risks to say, "We don't have material" or "This is the material that we have. This is all the material." I tend to sympathise with their position, but I also would certainly not be prepared to accept that at this late stage in the proceedings already, neither of them is in the position to at least disclose some material. It would take them a lot of persuasion to convince me that they are not in a position to do that. This is why rather than making an order and this is exactly my approach to you, and I hope you will appreciate it, rather than taking the rigid position myself and start making orders here and there, I'm putting until now my trust in your good judgement and in your sense of cooperation with each other, with one another and with the Tribunal, and I appeal to you to show me if you have any material which you can, in respect of the problems which you have mentioned, because I'm appreciative that you do have problems. I fully know that you have big problems. But still, I feel confident. I'm pretty sure that you have material that you can here and now disclose to the Prosecution and we can take it up from there, I mean without prejudice to other material that may become -- may come in your possession or which you may become aware of later on and which you undertake to disclose at a later stage without prejudicing the right of the Prosecution to be prepared herself in conformity with the basic principles of equality and parity of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hear what Your Honour says and I'm not going to press the matter further at this stage other than to say that past experience here of documents being produced at a late stage results in applications not surprisingly for adjournments so that the documents can be examined, and I would hope that if documents are produced at a late stage to the Prosecution, that Your Honour would be sympathetic to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ma'am, I can assure you that I will be sympathetic with whoever and whatever is reasonable. I have never expected miracles in -- from anyone in trials. I fully understand how busy you must be with this case as -- and I fully understand how much -- how busy the Defence team equally is busy, especially I fully understand also, and I don't want you to misunderstand me, that all along even though I have been on the bench for so many years, I realise that most of the time until the trial begins and sometimes until the trial comes to the stage where the Prosecution is closing, it's concluding its case, most of the time the Defence is somewhat not always at par with the Prosecution. My experience has taught me that the Prosecution has always got the edge over the Defence, particularly before the trial starts in that it has more time to collect -- to gather the evidence and to organise itself and especially in an environment like this where there has to be -- where there are translation problems and discovery sometimes, in particular, under Rule 68 takes the form of sending whole shipments to the Defence, the Defence may find itself in bigger problems than the Prosecution. I hope that you appreciate what I am saying because I repeat to you what I have just said to Madam Korner that you will find me reasonable when you are reasonable, and where there is justifiable -- not for an adjournment, but giving reasonable time for one to organise his or her efforts, I will do that. I also realise that as the trial unfolds, there will be surprises for everyone. There will be time when you are going to ask me for time to reorganise your own house, and there will be times when the Defence will be doing the same thing. You're not going to find me very difficult there if you are reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just mention, I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet again, but that's the point. Of course both sides will be asking for adjournments when unexpected things arise and that is why the rule is in place so that if there are documents of which the -- and I've heard Mr. Ackerman's response, that the Defence know that they're going to use and to sit on them until closer to a time when they are going to use them, in my submission, would be wrong and would require us to ask for adjournments that are not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There I fully agree with you in the sense that, and I'm sure -- Mr. Ackerman, you may sit down for the moment, I will spare you the -- as I understand it, and as I understand it should be, and I'm addressing Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Pitron as well as you. If Mr. Ackerman is aware of a piece of evidence that he may or may not choose to make use of at a later point in time, he does not have the option not to disclose it now. The moment he knows, he is aware of that piece of evidence, then he is duty-bound to disclose it to you. That is the situation. He is obviously free later on to organise his Defence the best way he chooses and as the need arises and as the trial unfolds, and he may actually decide not to bring forward some witness and that is his privilege and the Tribunal will not interfere with that privilege, just as it will not interfere with your privilege not to summon some witnesses that you have declared to now as being your intention to summon. That's your privilege. However, what I am doing now is to appeal to the Defence, in particular, at considering and acknowledging that you do have problems and acknowledging that certain documents you will discover the need for discovery at a later stage. If you have anything that you can make available to the Prosecution now, in good time, before the trial starts then you -- it is, by my conviction, that you should make it available. I will not make any orders now as requested by the Prosecution because I would rather prefer to make an order when I think that an order is definitely in place as we go further in time, and as I think the excuse or justification that you have brought forward today no longer holds water, then I obviously will make an order, but I will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse us, could the interpreters respectfully request a break. They need some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. I am --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think a break is being asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. I will close this argument and we will have a break for 20 minutes. Would that be okay with the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think you have taken my message and you will also make use of this 20-minute break to discuss it amongst yourself. I think some liaison between you is important. I'm not asking for the impossible, I am just asking for what is reasonable at the moment and I can assure you that if there is this kind of cooperation forthcoming from the Defence, you will find cooperation forthcoming from me when you need it at a later stage. That applies to you as well obviously. The sitting is suspended for the next 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I'm sorry. There's one matter before we leave the pre-trial briefs served by the Defence, which I had in a slightly different section. Does Your Honour have a copy of the one served by Mr. Ackerman available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in paragraph 2(G) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2(G), the documents emanating from ARC?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, we read it twice, and we just want to clarify, while Mr. Ackerman is here and so that Your Honour knows: Is that stating purely that except for certain exceptions, documents were not signed by Brdjanin, or is it saying that where the documents are, on the face of it, signed by Brdjanin, the signature of the -- the authenticity of the signature is disputed? Because if that's right, that raises an issue, and I wonder, if I could ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The vast majority of the documents are not signed by Mr. Brdjanin. Even though it appears to be his signature, it is not. And the Prosecution should notice that most of those have the word "za" preceding the signature, clearly indicating that it was signed by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, is it where the signature, excepting that not -- that a large number are not signed, but where the signature, on the face of it, appears to say "Radoslav Brdjanin" or "R. Brdjanin," is the Defence assertion that that is not his signature and someone has signed in his stead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's clearly the case. In fact, many of them will say "za R. Brdjanin" or "za Radoslav Brdjanin." That is -- "za" means for. Somebody is signing it for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that is different. I mean, I think, from what I can understand, with regard to these documents which state or purport to state at the end "for Brdjanin," you are alleging, if I read you well here, that, first, that "for" means that they were not signed by him; secondly is that they were not approved by him and/or were not issued with his knowledge or permission. This is what you are alleging. But the question that Ms. Korner has specifically put to you is a little bit different. She is asking you whether you are also alleging that in some documents you don't have "for Brdjanin," but Brdjanin's full name, Radoslav Brdjanin, purporting to be his own personal signature when in actual fact it's a forged one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe there are one or more documents of that character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think it's only fair to call upon you, if it is possible, between now and the commencement of the trial to identify those documents and indicate them to the Prosecution, because as you will certainly understand, there may be the need for a calligraphic expert or handwriting expert to establish the authenticity or otherwise of that signature as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would rather prefer to take the necessary steps at an early stage, or as early as possible, on that rather than leave it to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I leave it to you. I mean, I'm putting full trust in you, as I stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That should not be a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be one further request, and I make it. I didn't expect an answer, because obviously Mr. Ackerman will have to take instructions, and that is whether his client will agree to provide samples of his handwriting. As I say, I don't expect there to be an answer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't ask Mr. Ackerman to give an answer because I am sure that you may have other documents which contain the signature, what you consider to be the authentic signature of Radoslav Brdjanin and the comparison could be made with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the majority as with many of the -- many of the documents are photocopies and in my experience, I've no doubt Your Honours', experts would prefer to have an original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely but we come to that -- we cross that bridge when it's time. And I think you have got the messages and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have, and I'm even prepared to give the Prosecutor an answer and the answer is no it is the law of this Tribunal that we do not have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that's why I said I will not insist with you. Okay. Mr. Pitron, you will recall that Ms. Korner made specific mention of the Manjaca - pardon me if I don't pronounce the word correctly - Manjaca camp and the -- her complaint is that you did not, in your pre-trial brief, respond to her accusations with regard to this camp. So rightfully she would like you to make a statement now as to whether you are contesting the allegations of the Prosecution as contained in the indictment with regard to the Manjaca camp or whether your silence in that regard in your pre-trial brief means that you are accepting those facts or allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it seems to be that I wrote in the various submissions I have made, I contested all of the Prosecutor's allegations including those having to do with Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Incidentally, let me take advantage of the situation as it obtains at this very moment. You realise as much as I do that we are now with a fourth re-amended indictment. Basically when this case started way back, I don't remember when, you had both entered -- your client, your respective clients had both entered a plea of not guilty to the indictment, to the charges as they resulted from the indictment then on that occasion. Mr. Ackerman's pre-trial brief of the 16th of November in paragraph 1 states what to me is very obvious but I want to formalise it to be precise for the future. He starts his brief by stating that defendant Brdjanin had pleaded not guilty to the indictment, a plea which persists through successive amendments to the indictment and this is, according to me, how it should be. But I would like you just to formalise this matter once and for all before we start the trial to reiterate, if you feel it's the case of reiterating it, that each of your respective clients maintains the plea of not guilty even at this stage without prejudice, of course, to General Talic appeal, pending appeal on the decision of the 23rd of November with regard to the fourth amended indictment.
