I mean that is obviously without prejudice, remains without prejudice, but can I formalise that what Mr. Brdjanin's attorney stated in his pre-trial brief, namely that the plea persists, plea of not guilty persists throughout all the subsequent amendments, successive amendments to the indictment, can we record it in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you asking the defendant to actually rise again and say again that he's not guilty, or do you just want me to say on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to hear it from you first, in other words, that you are maintaining your position and also from Mr. Pitron so that I can actually ask your respective clients to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Our position is being maintained. He still maintains he's not guilty despite all the amendments to the indictment and makes that plea with regard to every amendment that has been made to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Pitron, always without prejudice to your other motions, pending motions, and also appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, may I just go back and correct one matter which Ms. Richertova has reminded me about disclosure. We are still receiving asked and unanswered documents from various sources and recently arrived was a criminal file in relation to what is colloquially known as the Mount Vlasic massacre, it's one of the ones mentioned in the killings. The file -- there was an investigation by the authorities. We asked for the file because we thought it would be important to the Defence. It's recently arrived so that will be coming their way as soon as we've managed to get it in some form of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you spell that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: V-l-a-s-i-c with an accent aigu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And one document arrived in relation to Bosanski Petrovac which will be disclosed as soon as we can get a translation done. I may say we're not sending it into the translation unit, we are going to try and get it translated within the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me jump now to the expert witnesses question. This was very briefly dealt with during the last Status Conference, and my recollection -- actually, it's not just a recollection, I don't think I need to remind you what the situation was. Your indication was that you intended to call something like 10 expert witnesses. You had mentioned one with regard, a historian. I mean what is the situation now? Do you still intend to call 10 expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- in fact, Your Honour, it will be eight. Dr. Donia who has given evidence in a number of trials, I've made inquiries because he will be the first witness but effectively most of what he will say has been said before. I hope to have his report by the end of this week to have a look at it and hope to get disclosure out. No other expert's report has yet been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically may I ask you what has been disclosed to the Defence so far with regard to expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No experts have been disclosed. Literally the reason is not that I am abiding by the 21-day rule which is the rule, but simply that we haven't had the reports. We mentioned the names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the 21-day rule basically, as I think I might as well tell you now, as I see it, doesn't mean a 21-day rule before the trial starts but it's a 21-day rule before you intend to summon that witness and -- but also you have -- or rather we have to make an allowance for further 14 days then which the Defence have a right to -- in case they want to cross-examine. So more or less the Tribunal will want to know beforehand, well beforehand that the Defence is being put in a position where they can inform the Court in good time whether they intend to have the expert witness cross-examined or not. That's very important. Secondly, one other thing that I felt I ought to hint at at this stage, and then obviously I do not intend to force it on either the Prosecution or on the Defence, but I am pretty sure that a substantial part of what you may want to prove by means of these expert witnesses may not be necessarily contested by the Defence. In other words, for example, there may be some historical events or some geographical details. I don't know exactly the details of what you want to prove by these expert witnesses. But if you think, between now and when the need to produce these expert witnesses arises, that there may be the possibility of asking for the cooperation of the Defence, and rather than bringing over experts and taking the time of the Court, of the Defence and yours, and involving also the Tribunal in unnecessary expenses, this same information could be obtained by direct reference to existing depositions in previous cases, provided there is the concurrence of the Defence, then perhaps we could contemplate that. Again, I do not intend to force anything on anyone at this stage in particular, but I am mentioning this because I realise that the case should be contested where it really is important to contest, and other matters which are not so fundamentally different, which should be the same for the Prosecution and for the Defence, on which there should be no dispute, I think I could rely on the cooperation of all parties later on. And I want you to realise that if you take this approach, you stand to gain, all of you. I mean, this is something which I hope I will convince you will be beneficial to each and every one of you there. There may be instances where I may have to put my foot down and ask you to curtail the number of witnesses that you intend to produce if I think that we are dealing with repetitive material, and I am sure that there are pieces of evidence which do not involve the -- do not implicate, directly or indirectly, any of the accused, which may not be contested by the Defence. If you could possibly identify these areas and come to some sort of pre-agreement with the Defence, that would be very much appreciated by the Tribunal. I know -- and I don't want you to tell me, "I have written to Defence counsel before and they did not have the decency or the courtesy to even reply." I don't want to hear it anymore. If it has happened, let's forget all about it. Start with a new page, as I said. I'm sure that Mr. Pitron and Mr. Ackerman are taking my message. There are instances when I would do exactly the same, believe me, but there are instances where I think it would pay me to be cooperative and economise on time, in particular, and also be practical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does actually bring me to one of the topics I wanted to raise first. In respect of experts, we will be giving the Defence the reports as and when they're ready to go rather than waiting. With Dr. Donia, really we intend to put in his report and deal with just the parts that we think are of the most relevance to the case, depending, of course, on how familiar Your Honours are with the history of the conflict and how much Your Honours would want to hear. That's the first matter. The second matter is this: We will be preparing a list of facts which we would invite the Defence to agree. It will be quite a lengthy list. It will be sent to the Defence, again, before Christmas, so that we'll give them the Christmas break to consider them. I would hope that, as Your Honour says, we can arrive at some agreement on facts which will not be contentious but merely are based upon, for example, rulings in other cases that have affected this area and the like. Your Honour, thirdly, on this topic, many, many of the witnesses that we have served deal with what has been come to be called the crime base, that is, the evidence of crimes committed which the Prosecution are adducing to show a pattern of events which cannot have come about by coincidence but by design. These witnesses, many of them, do not directly implicate the defendants. We have already adopted the procedure by which they have made declarations under the terms of Rule 92 bis. We have not yet heard from the Defence for General Talic on the matter. We have from Mr. Ackerman. Indeed, I found a fax during the break, effectively saying that at the present time, he hadn't fully considered all of them but that his view was that they would have to be called. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to about 70 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We've got 75, roughly, witnesses under this Rule. But Your Honour -- and we would obviously be addressing Your Honour if we cannot reach agreement, because it's Your Honour's ruling that matters. But even of the live witnesses, it would be helpful if the Defence could indicate if there are witnesses they will not require to attend because the witnesses do not implicate directly either of the accused, so that their statements may be read. Your Honour, we are as anxious as Your Honour, and I would imagine the accused, to complete this trial as expeditiously and, obviously, as fairly as possible. It's been waiting a long time to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- let me perhaps jump the gun for a while. How expeditiously this trial will be conducted depends, number one, on the style of each and every one of you and the conduct of either the Prosecution or of the Defence when it comes to examination-in-chief and cross-examination; secondly, and perhaps more importantly, on how much control I will be able to exercise upon you in the course of the trial, and I usually take the line of interfering as little as possible as long as you do not take advantage, undue advantage of the situation, and as long as you treat the witnesses as you should, with decorum and without abusing of the witnesses. Then you will find that I will interfere as little as I can. But what is perhaps more important is that each one of you ought to know beforehand what is the wheat and what is the chaff, and not produce in front of the Court material which you know is not an issue, is irrelevant, and which will only serve to prolong unduly the proceedings. I have every reason to believe, because this is what I have been told, that I am unlucky to have this case, but I am very lucky to have Mr. de Roux, Mr. Pitron, Mr. Ackerman, and you, and with all your respective teams, because you know your business well and that you shouldn't contribute towards an unnecessary and undue prolongation of this trial. And therefore, there I am hopeful. But I also know that it will serve this purpose: If you could do this before what you have suggested and seriously tackle it and try to keep an ongoing exchange of views on this before the trial begins. I think that is important. Because what frightens me is that you will send this list to the Defence and the Defence will take the rigid view of not responding or telling you no commitment. That's what I'm afraid of. I'm afraid of, not because I have reason to believe that that is what will happen. It's something that I have done in the past myself, you know. I mean, and probably you have done in the past as well. But something which perhaps there will be areas where it can be avoided in this case, so that we can get the case -- get this case started and proceed with an expeditious manner as possible. What worries me is the length of time that Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic have already been in custody. I want to reduce that time to the least possible and I want this trial to start. I can assure the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence that I will leave no stone unturned in making sure that there will be a fair trial, but the trial must start. Whatever you can do between now and the commencement of the trial to pave the way and make things easy or easier or less difficult will be appreciated. This is my message. Do you intend to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the Court will permit me, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First thing I want to say is that I'm perfectly willing to do that which the Court suggests and to make it unnecessary to put on evidence that really has nothing to do with the issues in the case. I'm in a bind, however, and I need the Court to understand that bind. If Ms. Korner were to hand me this list that she refers to today, and I've seen similar lists, I know what it's going to look like. I would have to say no I can't agree to any of that. The reason is this: I haven't counted, Your Honour, but I think there may be as many as 15.000 pages of material that has yet to be translated that I haven't been able to see yet and I would not want to say I agree to this proposition and then find a piece of evidence that totally contradicts it and I'm too late to do anything because I've already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- I won't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that but you will fully understand also that certainly I do not expect you to commit yourself to anything if you don't -- if you feel that in your client's interest you shouldn't do it. That's number one. But you, I am sure will also understand because we have lived trials, both of us, you will also understand that there will be -- the trial will develop in such a way that there will be a time when what you are not prepared to concede by way of a fact now or before, you will be able or you will be prepared to concede at that later stage, and be prepared because although you have now all the right to say no to each and every one of these question marks that Ms. Korner are going to ask you, is going to ask you to agree to or not to agree to, that the Court itself may, in due course, ask you, without any prompt from the Prosecution, whether it is possible to agree to this particular issue or this particular fact. I would not do it beforehand unless I, myself, am in the position to be able to -- to identify these facts and at the moment I am not like you are not, and I fully appreciate that you are not in a position to concede much or most of what you will be asking for. But there may be a time when you, please understand that the Court itself or the Tribunal itself will ask you whether you are prepared to concede, to agree to something that will be considered as not contentious by the Court. You may or may disagree, and I can put your mind at rest that if you don't agree, you will have it your way, but I will not be able to force it. What I will be able to force is the nonproduction of some witnesses if I think they are superfluous or irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want the Court to understand that if I say no to Ms. Korner about a number of things, it's not that I am obstructionist, it's that I'm not prepared yet because of all this material. And it's not her fault, it's the translation department that's causing all the trouble with this sort of thing. Then I think there was one other thing. Oh, with regard to Rule 92 bis, apparently things move slowly in the Prosecutor's office, but she has -- I have sent her three letters regarding 92 bis matters and I'm trying to move through those as rapidly as I can because I think they are of some urgency regard to the planning of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron, do you want to add anything or -- please go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got nothing further to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that topic, may I suggest it may be beneficial before the trial starts for there to be another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that. This is precisely what I was going to suggest. I am -- in the new spirit of cooperation that I have tried to build in the courtroom today and also because I have been making these appeals for further cooperation. It is my intention, and I am going to suggest to you that should you feel the need for it, and I think I will feel the need for it, I will offer you another pre-trial hearing before we start the trial; in other words in the -- the recess finishes on the 4th so we're talking as from the week which starts on the 7th onwards, and the earlier we hold it, the better it is. So that we can trash in that hearing the few areas which -- where perhaps we could find some ways of cooperation and other matters which we may not be able to conclude today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest that we supply Your Honour with a copy of the list of facts so Your Honour will have a chance to go through it. I would hope that we would be able -- Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Pitron and myself would be able to meet perhaps the day before to try and see where we can reach agreement. The difficulty, of course, with contact is everybody is in a different country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I would suggest is -- I mean but this is perhaps a choice which -- on which you could perhaps advise me yourselves. My basic instinct is to suggest a date which is very near the 21st of January and the expectation that maybe Defence counsel, in particular, because you are always here, but Defence counsel will probably arrive here in The Hague rather near the commencement of the trial than much earlier. So if that will be convenient to you, I'm in -- perhaps you could consult with one another between now and then and -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my plan is basically to move here January 7th or 8th, somewhere in that neighbourhood, so I would be available to the Court after that date. And the other thing that you need to understand is that I have a wife who wants me to speed up this trial much more than you probably do, so I think it may move rather rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My wife doesn't interfere in this. She has no interest anyway. Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Your Honour, I agree with that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... ask you to come and go on the Thalys every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I prefer to take the plane. The Thalys is not that easy. I would have some problems at the beginning of the week of the 7th, 8th, and 9th but I am prepared to make all efforts to ask Mr. de Roux to take my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be assured that the Court will try to accommodate you as much as the Tribunal -- I have a habit of referring to myself as the Court when I am no longer the Court. I will try to accommodate you as much as I can and this applies not only to this additional hearing that I am suggesting but also later on when we start the trial itself. I'll try to make your life easy because I know that the easier I make it for you, the easier it will make it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I could say the week of the 14th, like say Monday, the 14th of January, although I believe that's the Serb Orthodox New Year but -- so it may be that the two defendants would not wish to attend on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I know that the Orthodox Christmas comes either a week or two weeks later, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The trial was due to start on the 14th and it was pointed out that this was Serb Orthodox New Year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I have full respect for that if it is the wish of the defendants not to have a hearing on the 14th, I'll definitely not have a hearing on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 15th is the day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have it on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not have it on the 15th. 15th is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my knowledge of B/C/S tells me that he wants the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So Your Honour that will be most helpful if we could make that the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will have a confirmation of that in due course, and if you encounter difficulties in the meantime or you would like to have that date changed, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excuse me for the scheduling issue. The 16th might be a possible date also instead of the 15th. Could we think about the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am going to be here every day so I am the least of problems, and I promised you to accommodate you so if there is no problem on Mr. Ackerman's and Ms. Korner's side, I will have it on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I then just raise two other matters in advance. In the pre-trial brief served on behalf of General Talic, the specific mention, if Your Honour would like to find it of a challenge to the authenticity of specific documents. Your Honour, I wonder that if we could ask in advance of that hearing, we could be notified, given a list of the documents to which there is a specific challenge that they are not authentic because again, Your Honour, that raises all sorts of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Mr. Pitron, do you think that you would be in a position between now and the next time we meet?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible, but I think it's rather simple. I am challenging the authenticity of all the documents which are not signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so I understand, that is any documents emanating from the 1st Krajina Corps collection which do not bear General Momir Talic's personal signature, the authenticity is challenged; in other words, that they don't come from the 1st Krajina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can accept as probative value only one which is signed no matter what its source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it becomes a question of -- well, I think I understand his point. Then ultimately it's a question that has to be decided upon when the Tribunal comes to its decision. More or less what we are talking about, if I am reading him well, is that there are documents and documents. There are documents which are in their original and, therefore, the authenticity of those documents, the question of authenticity is more or less nonexistent or relative, and then there are documents which are unsigned and documents which are unsigned he is questioning. Now, they may be originals, they may be copies or photocopies of original documents. I think that's a question of -- that we have to encounter later on but it's not the same issue that was raised by ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it isn't the same issue. But it is not clear from that reply whether the fact that the suggestion is the documents not directly signed by General Talic came into existence at a later date or, alternatively, were never in -- may I tell Your Honour that the -- what I call the 1st Krajina Corps collection was seized from the building in 1998 and it's not clear whether it is suggested by General Talic that these documents were not there and have been obtained from somewhere else. And on that, I imagine that Mr. Pitron has clear instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think just keep alive the distinction between a matter of law and a matter of fact. I think basically the -- what he's referring to is a matter of law. According to him, every single document that is not signed by his -- purported to be signed by his client --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is not admissible. And therefore, he's -- that's how I read you. Do I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two things, Your Honour. There were the documents from my client, but there were all the other documents. For instance, as far as I can remember, there was a report or a brief from the Prosecutor from Teslic which isn't signed, which has not been authenticated by any source -- any seal, rather. There are pieces of sentences which are accusatory. I cannot accept this document as such without having the truth of the -- without proof of the truthfulness of the probative value of the document, which is different from the problem of those documents which are signed by my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, I think it reduces itself to something very fundamental that we encounter in most trials, that there may be the need for me or for the Chamber, as we go along and as Mr. Pitron raises in the various instances, to decide first of all on whether that particular document ought to be admitted from a legal point of view. Then the probative value of it and ultimately whether it will serve any purpose at all will be a matter to be decided -- will be a matter to be argued between you, but it will be a matter to be decided by whoever has to decide on the guilt or otherwise of ... I don't think it will create much problem, because he's making himself very clear. There is a bulk of documents that he's going to tell you straight away, from the very word "go", "These I do not acknowledge," but then it's up to the Tribunal to say whether they will be referred the Tribunal or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I fully understand that now. That means, however -- may I say, this is a very heavily document-based case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. It's frightening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm going to come on to the question of documents physically in a moment. That will mean that in each and every case, unless it is a document signed by General Talic, we will have to argue the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't necessarily agree to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You definitely - and I will stop short of saying more - you definitely will be required to bring forward evidence, and I would suggest you bring it as early as possible, to indicate what these documents are, where they were obtained from, how they were obtained, who came in possession of them in the first place. These are all important, because they have a bearing on the authenticity question. Then the authenticity aspect may widen. There may be documents from amongst this pile which we will not have problems about, and there may be documents which I myself might query, you know. I mean, for example, if it's a photocopy of a photocopy of a photocopy, I might myself come forward with problems for you, or for the Defence, for that matter, you know. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then, as I say, what we are proposing to do is serve a document which will show where each document we wish to produce comes from in the sense of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's important. It's like exhibiting a set of photographs, I mean, without producing the photographer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I would hope that we wouldn't have to produce the photographer for some of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, for my sake as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would then ask the Defence -- it may be quicker to ask which ones they do accept, by the sound of it, as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I can speak for Mr. Pitron. I don't think he is going to stand up and tell you, "I accept the authenticity of all documents which bear my client's signature," because he might come across one document, now or later, where Mr. Ackerman is going to tell you, "This is not my client's signature," and therefore, please don't expect from him to rise and tell you, "These I accept." All the others, a priori, he's contesting, and whether he's right and whether he'll be proven right or wrong, that's a matter that has to be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely. I understand the position that Mr. Pitron is taking at the moment. I simply want an indication of those that he will accept without any further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you prepared to give an indication of the documents that you will accept, Mr. Pitron?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the list which the Prosecutor will give to me, and in respect of the time available, I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then one of the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm taking that as a commitment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, so am I taking that as a commitment, yes. I will therefore be calling as one of the first witnesses the lead investigator to deal with as many as I can of those problems, because otherwise, Your Honour, if we have to stop and do this in respect of each particular municipality, we could be here a very long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, finally, Your Honour, is this: Documents for Your Honour and whoever your colleagues may be, if you know who they are already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there is an official document which states who the other two Judges will be, but it doesn't mean to say that when we come to the trial, those will be the two other Judges. Actually, it's a formality that is needed. At the present moment, the Chamber, as you know, is composed of Judge Schomburg, Judge Mumba, and myself, but I can tell you here and now, without revealing the names, which are not official in any case, but that this will not be the composition of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber will be different, because, as you know, each one of us will be dealing -- will be presiding over a trial. So Judge Mumba will be presiding over a trial, Judge Schomburg will be presiding over a trial, and I will be presiding over a trial, over this trial. And I will have two other Judges which I'm sure you're intelligent enough to conclude already they will not be Judge Schomburg or Judge Mumba, because they cannot be with me if they are presiding over another trial themselves. You will soon know who the other two Judges are. I haven't been formally informed. Informally, I have been told, but formally, not yet, so I don't think I am in a position to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a slightly throwaway line and I should know better. What I was attempting to say was: We propose to call evidence by municipality. We will prepare binders for Your Honours, if this is the way you would like it, with the documents as per the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a wise approach, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What we will do, Your Honour, is provide the Defence, because they have all these documents, with the numbers of the documents as per the municipality, so they can, if they wish, arrange their documents in that way. Your Honour, we did hear in one Trial Chamber that 15 copies were asked for of all documents. Your Honour, we would submit that puts an unreasonable burden. We would ask that we provide -- exactly, Your Honour, that the documents amount to some 40 binders already. Could we ask that we provide a copy for each -- for Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues and then one copy for the Court deputy, the Registry - I'm not sure who it is - but one, which makes a total of four?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I had to consult my Senior Legal Officer, because, as you imagine, I'm new to this regime. I am being advised that we will need one copy each, the three Judges, then one copy for the Senior Legal Officer, which the assistant legal officer will make use of as well, and one copy for the Chamber registrar, for the registrar, so that makes it five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Your Honour, then there's nothing else that I wish to raise at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But there are a few things that I need to raise. You mentioned at the last -- or rather, you didn't mention it, but my predecessor, during the last Status Conference, with reference to forensic evidence, to the matter of forensic evidence, suggested to the Defence to consider agreeing, amongst other things, but in particular, that formal proof of death , as opposed to the cause of death, could be dispensed with. Mr. Ackerman, I have it on record, was more or less agreeable to this. Mr. Pitron reserved his position on the grounds that he needed more time to consider what to reply to this. Because this would definitely spare us having to go through some material which -- I don't know, but the less I say, the better it is. If you need more time, Mr. Pitron, I am prepared to give you more time, but I appeal to you to understand the reason behind this -- not request; this accommodation. Mr. Ackerman first. Mr. Pitron will have more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give him more time to think about it. Judge Hunt outlined a procedure that was being used, I think, maybe in the Kordic case, where, as I recall -- I'd have to look at the transcript, but I think a witnesses would simply testify that a particular person was in a particular place and disappeared and has not been seen again, or that their body was recovered from a certain place or something, without going through all of this voluminous exhumation evidence, which I have no desire to hear and I think it furthers nothing. So I'm certainly willing to agree to a procedure that shortens up that process and accomplishes what needs to be accomplished in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem in respect of the fact that the exhumations took place or that there were deaths. Sometimes, but not often, I have some doubts in respect of the status of the different people. We've moved forward since the last time. I haven't completely finished thinking about that issue, but I think I should come to a decision very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And may I suggest to you - and I'm saying this to show you that when you cooperate, I cooperate - when you come forward later on, as Mr. Ackerman has, take it from me that you would still have reserved the right to ask for the production of evidence with any particular death related to any particular person, should you think it is necessary for the purposes of the defence you adopt for your client. In other words, this will be the general exemption, sort of, with this particular reservation: should the need arise. In other words, if you would agree to -- consider agreeing that the formal proof of that has happened generally, but if there is the need to ask for more details or to require evidence with regard to any specific case in particular, you will be free to do it. Okay? Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very clear exhumations is one of the matters that I was going to put on to the agreed facts. We've served schedules but we can simply call an investigator who's dealt with all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say is that they may say okay, we give a carte blanche with regard to all these allegedly dead persons or the persons that have disappeared except Mr. X, Mrs. Y, Mr. Z, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's only fair not to expect -- so okay. Next, witnesses –for whom the Prosecution’s latest motion for protective measures refers. Now, this was dealt with very briefly in the previous Status Conference. You have now filed a motion for protective measures. I don't think we need to go into details. I am waiting for a response, a reply from the Defence with regard to this motion. This will be dealt with in due course. We don't need to waste time today on it. Okay. However, I would like some light, I would like you to throw some light on whether you intend to seek protective measures such as pseudonyms, face, voice distortion or closed session with regard to other witnesses and whether you would be in a position to -- should you -- and I see you nodding so I assume that you do intend, should you -- should you be in a position to do this in good time before we start the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to -- what we are proposing to do with that is do it in batches because each witness may, at one stage say, "Yes, I do require protective measures," but then circumstances change or say, "No, I do not require," and then -- we are in the process of recontacting every witness on the list to check on the position. We will serve them in batches so before we intend to call the evidence, way before. We will be serving a motion right at the beginning of January for quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I just mention, Your Honour, the difficulty is that we had intended to start with Banja Luka but it may well be, I think from what Mr. Ackerman's saying, that we may have to start another municipality but we'll have to consider that matter in which case that affects the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a matter which I will definitely not interfere. The way you plan and conduct your case is your problem or your privilege.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, but if -- I think from -- but I will discuss the matter with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The matter of the Prosecution's most recent motion for protection is one that disturbs me a great deal and I feel obligated to say something about it but I want to do it in closed session. I don't want to say it publicly. And so I'm wondering if we could go into closed session right now for just a moment so I can address it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a matter for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I wanted to hear what you had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what Mr. Ackerman is going to say so I can't express ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I come along and we'll go into closed session now, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. During the last Status Conference, the Prosecution indicated its intention to request permission to tender transcripts of evidence given in other cases before this Tribunal, and it seems that it was hinted that -- or rather I would leave it at this: Do you still intend to seek permission to tender transcripts of evidence given in other cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I try to cover every aspect, but I must say this one I really don't know what the present situation is. I thought we had actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had mentioned it in your pre-trial brief as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Somebody's been dealing with and I'm afraid I haven't had a chance to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was not concluded. You just hinted that the intention was possibly to prove the existence or that there was an international armed conflict at the relevant times by means of transcript of evidence given in a previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm with you now, I'm sorry. We've disclosed to the Defence binders of documents relating to international armed conflict. I'm not sure that Mr. Ackerman responded. Mr. Pitron said they didn't accept any of it and we'd have to fight international armed conflict all over again is one of the matters I'd hoped we wouldn't have to fight but if we have to -- but we have served all those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now may I offer my services, and maybe I will succeed in reducing it to something which would be acceptable to both. Mr. Pitron, I put it to you or suggest to you to keep a distinction between the issue of the internationality of the conflict and the existence of the conflict itself. In other words, we will leave unprejudiced and something to be proven and debated by you the issue of the internationality of the conflict while we could, perhaps, agree to prove the existence of the conflict by means of a previous evidence tendered in other -- on a previous occasion in another trial. Would that be acceptable to you? Please, I'm just making a suggestion. If you don't agree, you don't agree and we'll move ahead, because basically what is important for you for the purposes of the accusations of the charges, internationality of it, I mean it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think if you want to move things forward, it would not be a good idea to deny the fact that there was a conflict. However, the internationality of the conflict does appear to me something which can be challenged because for me most of the time, for the most part it was a civil war so whatever the conclusions were in other trials in respect of other types of offences of individuals, I think that must be given very considerable study by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That brings me, before I ask you to take the floor, that brings me to the other related issue which was brought up last time, namely your -- you had foreshadowed sort of that you will be seeking or asking for this Tribunal to take judicial notice of adjudicated facts particularly those emanating from the Tadic case and if I did not misunderstand what the hint was, you were also hinting that this could also -- you suggested judicial notice would include also aspects on the internationality of the armed conflict. If we could agree that that is not the case, in other words, that you are not asking the Tribunal to take judicial notice of something which the Defence is very strongly objecting to and very strongly contesting, that is the internationality of the conflict, I think we can move ahead with eliminating most of the evidence that relates to the existence or the occurrence of the conflict itself and restricting your efforts to prove and debate merely then the aspect of the internationality of it. Without having it depend on what was decided in Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not only been decided in Tadic, it's been decided in a number of other cases. Your Honour, can I put it this way, it may not be the most urgent matter to decide in one sense. I'm not sure, but I believe there may be some kind of a rule change that's going to happen in respect of this taking of judicial notice which may have an effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honour, could we leave it until I believe that's going to be -- it will be in the next Plenary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I thought, Your Honour, and I think we may have a clearer idea then of what we can achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's more or less -- there's very little left. There is the aspect of the length of the trial which I think I can adjourn as an item on the agenda for the next meeting that we will have prior to the -- and there are certain rules or methods of conducting the relations between the Prosecution and the Defence that I would like you to adopt as we go along and that is more or less -- I would like you to prepare on a rolling basis obviously in good time for and -- the order of witnesses that you intend to follow so that the Defence will be placed in the position where they will not have any reason to complain. I would like you also to give particular attention to the list of exhibits that you intend to produce and again, I have already heard a complaint from Mr. Ackerman in regard to this. I would like you to streamline it as much as you can and make things easy. And then I may be suggesting something which you have already decided upon, but I was going to suggest to you possibly to organise the exhibits and the list of exhibits by municipality, if you can do that. If it's not convenient for you, then I am prepared to listen to what you have to say and will interfere as little as I can. But what I want is to try and have things organised before we start and as we go along, so that things will be easy for you, for the Tribunal, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think -- Your Honour, I hoped I'd made it clear. The exhibits will be organised into municipality binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I suggest that whatever happens, the numbering doesn't change, because otherwise it's going to confuse everybody if we start having to change the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The numbers have to remain the same. I have already -- actually, when I was discussing this with my staff, I already made it -- it's important. I mean, otherwise there will be ... It has been suggested to me to suggest to you something --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dare we ask who by?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- which I think is very important. I think it is very important. I'm referring to witness testimony sheets. I'm told -- I haven't had experience of this as yet, and therefore you will pardon me for this, but I'm told that a problem often arises in cases when the identity of a witness protected by a pseudonym is incidentally or unwittingly disclosed by another witness who refers to them by their full name during the course of a particular testimony. The suggestion made to me in order to get around this problem is that the Defence and the Prosecution should prepare a witness testimony sheet that lists the names and pseudonyms of protected witnesses. I'm reading, actually. This sheet should be the first thing given to the witness, and at the commencement of his or her testimony, and the witness should be told that if they need to refer to anyone on that list, they should do so by using the pseudonym indicated. Do you consider this as a practical suggestion? Do you have any reservation to it or do you see any inherent danger in resorting to such a list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I give precedence to age, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Generally, the protection is to be protected from knowledge that they are testifying as witnesses in this Tribunal, not that they have some knowledge of events that occurred. So if a witness were to say, "I was at such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time and Joe Smith was also there," if Joe Smith is a protected witness, that's not a problem, because that doesn't disclose that Joe Smith is a witness in this trial. But if the witness were to say, "I was at the hotel last night and Joe Smith, another witness, and I went out and had a drink," that's a whole different matter. That discloses that he is a witness at the trial. So I think it's things that disclose what is protected that are important to be protected, not becoming completely crazy about that proposition, and so I'd certainly go along with that kind of a process if what we're doing is following what the protection is, and it never is that one may never know that this person was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know where the suggestion comes from, because I've been taking part in the trial in which it's been happening. Your Honour, I think, in fact, what was happening in that trial is that if a protected witness is a protected witness, then whenever he's referred to, he's referred to by those initials, whether it's "I met him in the hotel where I'm staying" or whether it was at the scene of the incident. I think we can discuss this, but I know the type of sheets Your Honour is thinking of, and it does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not thinking of. This is a suggestion that has been made to me. I have put it to you because obviously I would like to hear what you have to say on it. Mr. Pitron, would you like to say something about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I render tribute to the aged experience of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's a matter that you can take up amongst yourselves later on, and I think I can for the moment bring this Pre-Trial Conference to an end and adjourn other matters that I had in mind of bringing up to the next Pre-Trial Conference, which will be held on the 16th and not on the 15th, and we can conclude by now reverting to a very short Status Conference, which we are, by Statute ... If we can summon it now and conclude it very quickly, then we'll do it. Otherwise we will have to take a break of 30 minutes and come back after 30 minutes and have the Status Conference. Frankly, I don't know what we could add. The only thing is that I want to make sure that your respective clients do not have any remarks or complaints to make in relation to their state of detention. That is something that I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. No complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I still see you standing up, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm hoping we're not completely finished with the Pre-Trial Conference, because I did have a couple of things that I did want to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can mention them and then we will deal with them on the 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This one is very important. I really would like -- if you don't know, then it's fine. You can tell me you don't know. You know, I'm -- I'm a sole practitioner in Texas, and so I have to make arrangements for what goes on with my practice while I am here. Now, in the last case that I tried here, we generally followed a two-week-on-two-week-off schedule, so that I was able to go back to the US and take care of business in the US during those interims. I have no idea what kind of a schedule the Chamber has in mind for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no idea either as yet, but I told you beforehand I will try to accommodate you as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore, this is something that we could perhaps discuss at a later stage. The important thing, Mr. Ackerman, is that we start the trial and that we get moving, and this is why I'm appealing to you -- when I say "you," it's not you, Mr. Ackerman, or you, Mr. Pitron, or you, Madam Korner. When I say, "you," it's all of you. This is why I'm appealing to you to be as constructive and as cooperative as possible, because the more you are cooperative, the shorter the trial will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you've been a judge and a lawyer long enough, and have I, to know that prepared lawyers try cases faster than unprepared lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so that when we need time for preparation, we need time for preparation, and we can make the case move faster. And I think our experience in Celebici was that those two-week-on-two-week-off sessions actually made the trial move a bit faster. Probably three weeks on, one week off would have worked if we had had the courtroom but we didn't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's probably what -- I'm not -- almost thinking aloud, but I will not be surprising you at all if I told you that that is what I more or less had in mind, three weeks on, one week off. That's what I had in mind. But then it depends, because it could well happen that we get stuck after one week and we need to take a week off. So this is why I'm telling you I will accommodate you. I mean, I will -- I know that everyone is busy, everyone has got -- we'll see how this works. If we need to stay in any particular moment for four weeks, we will do it, but then obviously we will need to stop as the need arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding of what was going to happen -- I'm sorry. I thought Mr. Ackerman had finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I had finished with that issue. The other issue -- you basically covered most of everything else. You mentioned that you would like the Prosecutor to give us advance notice of the witness order, and I would hope that that could happen as soon as possible, because we do have work to do because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I mean, please make an allowance also to what Ms. Korner has said today, that she might feel the need to change her plan and, instead of starting with the Banja Luka municipality, start with something different. I also heard you say that it makes more sense to start with the Banja Luka municipality rather than with something else. My role here is minimal. I have learnt to keep my mouth shut in such instances. What I can tell you is: If you can sit down together and eliminate or reduce the problems that would make it safer for the Prosecution to start with another municipality rather than Banja Luka, so that she can start with Banja Luka, then I think you can sit down and do it. I mean, I understand that the problem may be the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a huge problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can -- I understood that the diary -- the translation of the diary could be a problem relating to -- depending on if you could start with Banja Luka municipality or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Can I just say -- it really is -- it's not so much my problem. I intend at the moment to start with Banja Luka, having ready by the 21st, we understand, the 300 translated pages that it's now come down to. But as I said, it will really depend if Mr. Ackerman objects to that, and on the basis that he's not in a position, maybe, to properly cross-examine witnesses I'm going to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but by the time we start the trial and the preliminaries, by the time we get to the first witness, substantive witness. I mean, if you regulate the production of the witnesses in an intelligent way, as I have reason to believe you will do, then in the meantime there will be again ample time. This is why I would like to sit down together. And I understand it may be difficult, but -- or it may be difficult the first time, but you may be surprised to find how easy a solution comes along. Especially if you want to find one, you will find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am really entirely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because in a trial, you know more than I do, that if you have a hundred witnesses, they are not going to give evidence on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, but I -- can I make it absolutely clear? The only thing that would prevent me starting with Banja Luka would be if Mr. Ackerman were to say, "I cannot cross-examine the witnesses that you have on your list from Banja Luka who are all listed because we don't have the full diary translated." As I say, as I know that he has B/C/S speakers and readers on the team, and the defendant can read it, which is more than we can, I would have hoped that he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but let me overstep my role as a Judge for a moment, and I'm sure Mr. Ackerman will forgive me for this genuine intrusion. I am sure you know that if you are not in a position to cross-examine a witness, a particular witness, or more than one witness, at any given time because the full translation of the diary, this famous diary, is not yet in your possession, and then later on, when it's in your possession, you ask for the cross-examination, you can reserve the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can reserve the cross-examination. And if that is the case, you will make the life of the Prosecutor easier in the sense that if she thinks that it is more logical and makes more sense to start with the Banja Luka municipality, and you seem to agree with that, then she can start with that and there will be a reservation made, and then I'm sure you will use your good sense. I mean, you're not going to take advantage of it or abuse the facility of reserving cross-examination. You'll cross-examine when you can cross-examine, there and then, and you will reserve, and the Court will meet you, not halfway but full way, when it is reasonable and necessary to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the matter is very clear. I do not presume to tell the Prosecutor how to put on their case. That's their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if they want to start with Banja Luka, I won't object to that. Judge Hunt has entered an order regarding my objection with regard to Witness 207, and I'm relying on that. He has said and that and the Prosecutor has agreed that that witness will be called very close to the end of the case so that I will have all that material when I have to cross-examine that witness, and if any witnesses who testify before that time need to be recalled for additional cross-examination because of the contents of that diary, then that will happen and I'm totally satisfied with that. That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I think at this stage let's leave it at that although there may be problems if cross-examination is reserved and witnesses have to come back again from places. Some of the places are more difficult than others. But can I just mention on the scheduling my understanding was that the idea would be that we would be sitting every day for half days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- yeah. That's what I have been told. The idea is as Judge Hunt pointed out to you in the last Status Conference that as from January, there will be six trials being heard simultaneously; obviously three in the morning, three in the evening or afternoon evening. There is no hard and fast rule on the basis of which I can tell you the Brdjanin/Talic case will always be held in the afternoon or always in the morning because this will be alternating there will be weeks when we will work in the morning, weeks when we will work in the afternoon. This is depending on the scheduling, general scheduling that is prepared by -- not by me, but by the Registry of the Tribunal. Of course you will know beforehand, this is not something that's going to be announced the day before. You are not going to be told the day before, "Tomorrow we work in the morning," and then you don't know the day after tomorrow whether you are working in the morning or the afternoon. This will be something that you will know about, I hope, but I have been told that there is no hard and fast rule meaning that one trial will always be held in the morning, one trial will always be held in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, and indeed I would hope that it would be one week it might be in the afternoons and the next in the morning because it makes life a little bit easier, but what concerns me is Your Honour seems to be agreeing with Mr. Ackerman that we'd sit three weeks with one week off. Now, that will extend this trial quite a lot if we are only sitting something in the region of four hours a day, a half day, which is what it's going to amount to then we stop for a whole week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been assured by the Registrar that it won't change anything. I mean I personally fail to understand how it won't change anything, if you want the truth from me, but I've still got to find someone who had shed enough light but anyway, we'll organise ourselves and we'll plan as we go along. I mean for the moment, we can only plan on the short haul and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My concern is simply that the trial doesn't run so long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My concern is I share that concern. It's exactly like yours and I mean to throw my weight. Judge Hunt, my predecessor, has said, "my considerable weight." Mine is not that considerable, but whatever it is, I mean to throw it in an effort to get this trial over and done with in the shortest time possible and I am sure that I will find your full cooperation. I think I can close the Status Conference here as well and my apologies to the interpreters if I have abused of you today. It's my first time, you will forgive me. I promise you that next time I will be more understanding -- I shall be more understanding and will cooperate more with you but at least you don't have to come again after the 30 minutes break that was suggested. I thank you all and I look forward as I stated earlier to a shorter than expected trial. We will discuss this at the next conference which will be on the 16th of January and by that time, I hope that you would have cleared up further terrain making it common terrain for you to tell me that I can rely more and more on your cooperation for what I intend to be an exemplary trial. I thank you all. Good evening.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Pre-Trial Conference adjourned at
